pos: n. (a town of the Judean lowland, named once, in the second of Solomon's twelve commissariat districts)
etymology: Hebrew Maqats, probably an end or a boundary, from a root meaning to cut off; named once in Scripture, at 1 Kings 4:9.
biblical_def: Makaz is a town of the lowland named exactly once in all of Scripture, in the register of the twelve officers Solomon set over Israel to victual his household: “The son of Dekar, in Makaz, and in Shaalbim, and Bethshemesh, and Elonbethhanan” (1 Kings 4:9). Its site is unknown; nothing happened there that the Holy Ghost saw fit to record, and no prophet ever preached in it. It survives in the canon as one line-item in an administrative list. That list is itself instructive. Solomon's kingdom was at its height, and the measure of that height which Scripture gives is not a monument but a supply schedule: “And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). The daily reckoning follows — “And Solomon's provision for one day was thirty measures of fine flour, and threescore measures of meal” (1 Kings 4:22) — and behind that figure stand the fields of places like Makaz. The glory of Israel in her best days rested on the ordinary labour of towns whose names we cannot even locate, and the people of those towns are described in the same chapter as “eating and drinking, and making merry” (1 Kings 4:20). God keeps the names of obscure places in His book. That is the doctrine of this entry.

corruption_summary: Obscure places and obscure people are treated as filler in Scripture, when the Holy Ghost records them because He knows and keeps them.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader skips the lists. Makaz is in a list, and a list is precisely where God is most obviously keeping account of what no one else bothered to count. The administrative chapters of Kings and Chronicles are not padding left over from a palace archive; they are inspired record, and the names in them are names God chose to preserve when far grander things have perished without a trace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Lord numbers and names what the world considers too small to record, and that the prosperity of a kingdom rests on the daily labour of towns no one remembers.

pos: n. (a town of Judah resettled after the Babylonian captivity, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Mekonah, a base or a foundation, from the root kun, to establish; named once in Scripture, at Nehemiah 11:28.
biblical_def: Mekonah is a town of the south of Judah, named once, in Nehemiah's roll of the villages reoccupied by the returned captives: “And at Ziklag, and at Mekonah, and in the villages thereof” (Nehemiah 11:28). The name means a base or a foundation, from the verb to establish, and no name could suit the chapter better. Nehemiah 11 is the record of a people being set back upon their foundations. The holy city had to be repopulated by lot, because men would not willingly leave their fields for a ruined capital: “And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities” (Nehemiah 11:1). The remaining nine parts went out to places like Mekonah, and the chapter names them one after another — Kirjatharba, Dibon, Jekabzeel (Nehemiah 11:25), then Zanoah and Adullam and Lachish and Azekah, “And they dwelt from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom” (Nehemiah 11:30). The restoration was not a single dramatic act but the slow reoccupation of a hundred small foundations. That is how God generally restores a people: village by village, by the plain obedience of men who went where the lot sent them.

corruption_summary: Restoration is imagined as a dramatic event rather than the unglamorous reoccupation of ordinary ground, which is what Nehemiah 11 records.
corruption_paragraphs: A people expecting revival to arrive as a single spectacle will not recognise it when it comes as a list of villages. Nehemiah 11 is the shape of real restoration: lots cast, families moved, fields worked again, a hundred small foundations rebuilt by men whose names appear once. The rebuilding of a wall gets the attention; the repopulating of Mekonah is the harder and longer work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God restores His people by ordinary obedience in ordinary places, and that a man sent to a village has been sent by the same hand that assigned the rulers to Jerusalem.

pos: n. (a quarter of Jerusalem, the merchants' district, named once, in Zephaniah's oracle of judgment)
etymology: Hebrew Maktesh, a mortar or a hollow, the stone bowl in which grain is pounded; named once in Scripture, at Zephaniah 1:11.
biblical_def: Maktesh is a district of Jerusalem named once, and named only to be howled over: “Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the merchant people are cut down; all they that bear silver are cut off” (Zephaniah 1:11). The word means a mortar — the hollowed stone in which grain is pounded with a pestle — and it was evidently the name of a hollow or basin within the city where the traders kept their shops. The name is the sentence. A quarter called the Mortar is to be pounded. Zephaniah's oracle moves through the city gate by gate: “there shall be the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills” (Zephaniah 1:10), and then God turns His search upon the comfortable: “I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil” (Zephaniah 1:12). That is the sin of the merchants' quarter — not trade, which Scripture nowhere condemns, but the settled practical atheism of men whose money has persuaded them that God does nothing. The answer comes in the same chapter: “Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath” (Zephaniah 1:18).

corruption_summary: Practical atheism among the prosperous is treated as a private opinion, when Zephaniah names it as the sin for which a whole quarter is pounded.
corruption_paragraphs: “The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil” is the creed of men settled on their lees, and it is held far more widely than it is confessed. It is not argued for; it is assumed by the comfortable, who go on buying and selling as though the God who owns the market had retired from it. Zephaniah does not treat this as an intellectual position to be answered but as a sin to be punished, and he names the address where it was kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that silver and gold deliver no man in the day of the LORD'S wrath, and that a settled sense of God's indifference is among the most dangerous conditions a prosperous people can reach.

pos: n. (a stronghold of Moab, named once, in Jeremiah's oracle against that nation)
etymology: Hebrew Misgab, a high place, a refuge or a stronghold, from the root sagab, to be high or inaccessible; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 48:1.
biblical_def: Misgab appears once, in the opening verse of Jeremiah's long oracle against Moab: “Against Moab thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Woe unto Nebo! for it is spoiled: Kiriathaim is confounded and taken: Misgab is confounded and dismayed” (Jeremiah 48:1). The word means a stronghold or a high refuge — the same noun is used elsewhere of the LORD Himself as the high tower of His people — and here it stands as the proper name of a Moabite fortress. The irony is the point of the verse. The place called the Stronghold is confounded and dismayed. Moab's whole case is tried in that chapter and found to rest on two things, neither of which held: her possessions and her god. “For because thou hast trusted in thy works and in thy treasures, thou shalt also be taken: and Chemosh shall go forth into captivity with his priests and his princes together” (Jeremiah 48:7). A god who goes into captivity with his own priests is no refuge, and a fortress named Refuge is only a name. The charge is stated plainly at the end: “And Moab shall be destroyed from being a people, because he hath magnified himself against the LORD” (Jeremiah 48:42). The one true Misgab is the LORD, and a nation that will not have Him for a high tower will have none.

corruption_paragraphs: Moab had a fortress called the Stronghold, and it was confounded and dismayed. The lesson is not that walls are useless but that a name is not a defence and a treasury is not a refuge. Jeremiah 48:7 puts the two false confidences side by side — works and treasures — and a people trusting either will discover in one day that both were names only.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD alone is the high tower of His people, and that the nation or the man who magnifies himself against Him has no stronghold left, whatever the sign over the gate says.

pos: n. (a town on the appointed northern border of Canaan, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Ziphron, probably fragrance or a sweet smell; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 34:9.
biblical_def: Ziphron is named once, as a marker on the northern boundary God drew for the inheritance of Israel: “And the border shall go on to Ziphron, and the goings out of it shall be at Hazarenan: this shall be your north border” (Numbers 34:9). The whole chapter is a survey, and it is a survey God dictated before Israel had set a foot inside the land. “Command the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land of Canaan; (this is the land that shall fall unto you for an inheritance, even the land of Canaan with the coasts thereof:)” (Numbers 34:2). The borders are run point by point — “And this shall be your north border: from the great sea ye shall point out for you mount Hor” (Numbers 34:7), then to the entrance of Hamath and Zedad (Numbers 34:8), then Ziphron, then Hazar-enan. Ziphron's site is not known with certainty. What is certain is the doctrine the chapter carries: the inheritance of God's people is a surveyed inheritance, measured and bounded by God Himself and not by the reach of their swords. The land was a gift with corners in it, and the corners were marked before the conquest began.

corruption_summary: The land promise is spiritualised into a general sense of blessing, when Numbers 34 gives it as a surveyed territory with named corners.
corruption_paragraphs: A promise with corners in it cannot be reduced to a feeling of favour. God named the points of the northern line — mount Hor, the entrance of Hamath, Zedad, Ziphron, Hazar-enan — before Israel crossed Jordan, and the specificity is the comfort. What God gives, He measures; what He measures, He defends; and the inheritance of the saints in light is no less definite for being presently unseen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the bounds of His people's inheritance, and that the exactness of His promises is a mercy and not a technicality.

pos: n. (a town on the eastern border of Zebulun's inheritance, named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ittah Qatsin, commonly read as the time or the hour of a ruler, or as a town of the judge; named once in Scripture, at Joshua 19:13.
biblical_def: Ittah-kazin is named once, as a point on the line that bounded the inheritance of Zebulun: “And from thence passeth on along on the east to Gittahhepher, to Ittahkazin, and goeth out to Remmonmethoar to Neah” (Joshua 19:13). The name is commonly taken to contain the Hebrew word for a ruler or a judge, so that the place was perhaps the seat of a local chief. Nothing else is recorded of it. It belongs to the great survey of Joshua 13 to 21, in which the land is parcelled out tribe by tribe and village by village. The third lot fell to Zebulun: “And the third lot came up for the children of Zebulun according to their families: and the border of their inheritance was unto Sarid” (Joshua 19:10). From Sarid the line runs east “toward the sunrising unto the border of Chislothtabor, and then goeth out to Daberath, and goeth up to Japhia” (Joshua 19:12), and so by Ittah-kazin to the sea of Chinnereth country. The chapter ends with the plainest possible statement of what all this detail is for: “This is the inheritance of the children of Zebulun according to their families, these cities with their villages” (Joshua 19:16). God gave families addresses.

corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 13 to 21 is the least-read stretch of the Old Testament and one of the most doctrinally weighty, because it is the promise to Abraham turned into surveyed ground with the names of villages on it. Readers who want the land promise in the abstract find the survey dull; readers who want it kept find every obscure name in it a witness that God did not keep His word approximately.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives families addresses, and that a promise honoured in such detail may be trusted in the parts not yet seen.

pos: n. (a town north of Shiloh, named once, in the account of the wives taken for Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Lebonah, frankincense, from laban, to be white; named once in Scripture, at Judges 21:19.
biblical_def: Lebonah is named once, and only to fix the position of Shiloh for a grim piece of business at the end of the book of Judges: the feast at which the men of Benjamin were told to seize wives from among the dancing daughters of Shiloh. The elders locate the place with care — a yearly feast of the LORD in Shiloh, north of Bethel, east of the highway from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah (Judges 21:19). The name means frankincense, the white resin burned in worship, and it sits in the text next to one of the ugliest expedients in Israel's history. Benjamin had been all but destroyed, and the tribes had sworn an oath that forbade them to give their daughters; so rather than repent of a rash oath they contrived a theft: “then come ye out of the vineyards, and catch you every man his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin” (Judges 21:21). The men who devised it had wept before God and asked, “O LORD God of Israel, why is this come to pass in Israel, that there should be to day one tribe lacking in Israel?” (Judges 21:3). The book's own verdict closes the chapter: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25).

corruption_summary: The closing chapters of Judges are read as an embarrassment to be explained away rather than as Scripture's own indictment of self-rule.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers uncomfortable with Judges 21 try either to justify the elders or to discredit the book. Scripture does neither. It records the expedient in full, including the weeping that preceded it, and then passes sentence in its own words: every man did that which was right in his own eyes. The sin is not hidden and it is not excused; it is reported, and the reporting is the rebuke.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a rash oath is to be repented of rather than worked around, and that a nation without a true king will find its own conscience an unreliable judge.

pos: n. (a town or clan of Judah, named once, in the genealogy of Shelah's sons)
etymology: Hebrew Lekah, of uncertain meaning, perhaps a going or a journey; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:21.
biblical_def: Lecah is named once, in the Chronicler's register of the house of Judah: “The sons of Shelah the son of Judah were, Er the father of Lecah, and Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21). In this form of Hebrew genealogy a man is called the father of a town as readily as of a son, so Lecah is most likely a place founded or held by Er's descendants. What makes the passage worth a reader's time is the trade attached to it. These were the linen-workers of Judah, and the next verses add the potters: “These were the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1 Chronicles 4:23). The Chronicler keeps the names of craftsmen in the sacred record alongside the names of kings, and he pauses over the whole cluster with a phrase that reads like a scribe laying down his pen: “And these are ancient things” (1 Chronicles 4:22). Shelah himself was the third son born to Judah by the Canaanitess, and his birth is recorded at Gen 38:5 — “And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah”. From that unpromising household came weavers and potters who served the king.

corruption_paragraphs: The sacred genealogies name the men who wrought fine linen and the men who made pots, and name them as a matter of record worth preserving. A church that treats vocation as a neutral backdrop to real spiritual life has lost something the Chronicler assumed: that a man's craft is part of what God has given him and part of what God records of him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps the names of craftsmen, and that honest work done for the king is work the Holy Ghost saw fit to write down.

pos: n. (a town of southern Judah, named once, among the places to which David sent of the Amalekite spoil)
etymology: Hebrew Rakal, traffic or trade, from a root meaning to go about as a trader; named once in Scripture, at 1 Samuel 30:29.
biblical_def: Rachal is named once, in the list of towns to which David sent presents out of the spoil recovered from the Amalekites: “And to them which were in Rachal, and to them which were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to them which were in the cities of the Kenites” (1 Samuel 30:29). The name means traffic or trade. The episode behind the list is one of the finest things recorded of David before his accession. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families of his men; “And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives” (1 Samuel 30:18). What he did with the plunder is the point. He did not keep it, and he did not divide it only among the four hundred who fought. He sent it out to the elders of the towns that had sheltered him in his outlaw years: “Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD” (1 Samuel 30:26), and the list runs on to Hebron “and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt” (1 Samuel 30:31). A man about to be made king paid his debts to the obscure places that had fed him when he was nobody. Rachal is one of those debts, repaid and recorded.

corruption_summary: Gratitude to those who helped a man in obscurity is treated as optional sentiment rather than as the plain duty David discharged by name and by town.
corruption_paragraphs: David's distribution of the spoil is not generosity in the abstract; it is a debt paid to specific towns that had taken risks for a hunted man. The modern instinct of the successful is to forget the obscure places that carried them, and to call the forgetting moving on. Scripture records the list, which is to say it records the names of the creditors and the fact that they were paid.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that spoil taken from the enemies of the LORD is to be shared out, and that a man rising in the world owes a plain and nameable debt to those who sheltered him when he had nothing.

pos: n. (a place near Ramah with a great well, named once, where Saul asked after David)
etymology: Hebrew Seku, probably a lookout or a watch-place, from a root meaning to look out; named once in Scripture, at 1 Samuel 19:22.
biblical_def: Sechu is named once, as the place where Saul stopped on the road to Ramah and asked where his son-in-law was hiding: “Then went he also to Ramah, and came to a great well that is in Sechu: and he asked and said, Where are Samuel and David? And one said, Behold, they be at Naioth in Ramah” (1 Samuel 19:22). The name probably means a lookout, and the well there was evidently a known landmark. The scene is one of the strangest in the book. David had fled to the one man in Israel who had anointed him: “So David fled, and escaped, and came to Samuel to Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and dwelt in Naioth” (1 Samuel 19:18). Saul sent messengers and they prophesied; he sent more and they prophesied; at last he went himself, asked his way at the well of Sechu, and was taken by the same Spirit: “And he went thither to Naioth in Ramah: and the Spirit of God was upon him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah” (1 Samuel 19:23). The chapter ends with the proverb this produced: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Samuel 19:24). A man may be overruled by the Spirit of God in his body and still be a reprobate in his heart.

corruption_summary: Extraordinary spiritual experience is taken as evidence of a right heart, when Saul prophesied on his way to commit a murder.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul prophesied. He was overruled by the Spirit of God in the body, in public, so that a proverb was made of it, and he went on being the man who threw spears at David. The charismatic claim that unusual manifestation proves standing with God is answered in this chapter without any need for further argument: the Spirit of God may restrain and even use a reprobate, and the man will be no nearer heaven for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the test of a man is repentance and faith and not manifestation, and that God is perfectly able to stop an enemy in his tracks without saving him.
